one_liner: Go CLI that archives a directory tree into N independent tar files in parallel, much faster than GNU tar on parallel filesystems.
what_it_does: ptar walks an input directory and spreads its entries across N worker goroutines, each writing its own valid GNU-format tar file (prefix.0.tar, prefix.1.tar, ...); untarring all of them recreates the original tree. It is a command-line tool (ptar -c -t N -f prefix input), not a library and not a drop-in for tar's single-archive output. Optional per-file index files (offset, size, SHA-1, name) and gzip or lz4 compression per output file.
how_it_is_fast: Scan and archive are decoupled: one godirwalk walker (unsorted readdir) feeds paths into a 1024-slot channel, and N goroutines each lstat, open, read and append files to their own archive/tar writer. On a parallel filesystem such as GPFS the gain comes from keeping many metadata and read requests in flight at once, which serial GNU tar cannot do; there is no special I/O technique (plain os.Read with a 4 KiB buffer).
when_to_use: Archiving large trees (tens of thousands to millions of files) from parallel or network filesystems (GPFS, Lustre-style) where per-file latency, not bandwidth, dominates
HPC data migration or backup where splitting the output into many tar files is acceptable or even useful (partial recovery if one file is corrupted)
Uncompressed or lz4 archives, where the README's 10 TB run took 44m39s at 32 workers vs 10hr20m for GNU tar
Hosts with many cores and enough filesystem concurrency to feed 32-64 workers (the kernel-source run stopped improving past 64)
when_not_to_use: You need a single archive file or a pipe to stdout; output is always N separate tar files
Single local SSD or small trees: the 1-worker run (6m33s) was slower than GNU tar (6m4s), and nothing shows gains on local disks
Extraction speed matters: parallel decompression is listed as not done; you untar each piece yourself
Archives needing hard-link detection, sparse files, xattrs or ACLs: the code builds headers with Go's tar.FileInfoHeader only and does none of this
Production-critical jobs: abandoned since 2019, no tests, and any lstat/open/read error panics the whole process

integration.form: module (Go command-line tool, static binary via Makefile)
integration.min_toolchain: Go (GOPATH-era layout, no go.mod; a modern Go toolchain needs go mod init first); version not documented
integration.platforms: Unix-like (static CGO_ENABLED=0 build); tested only on Linux with GPFS per README
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (CLI); each worker owns its tar writer, shared state is channels only
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial - output tar files are GNU-tar readable, but the CLI and one-archive-per-run model differ from tar

gotchas: The code accepts --compression gz, not gzip (the CLI hint says gzip, which panics 'Not implemented'), and names outputs prefix.N.targz or prefix.N.tarlz4 with no dot before the compression suffix
Entry names are the paths as walked, so an absolute input path yields absolute names inside the tar (GNU tar would strip the leading /)
A file that disappears or is unreadable between scan and archive panics and aborts the whole run, leaving partial tar files
Files are dealt to workers in channel order with no size balancing (TarMaxSize is declared but unused), so output files can be very uneven
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling creates archives; fcp, wcp and uring-sync parallelize copying instead, and hop speeds up reading single files from an archive. Pick ptar when the goal is getting a huge tree on a parallel filesystem into tar files fast and N output files are acceptable.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README tables only: on GPFS with a hot page pool, archiving the 1.5 GB, 47K-file Linux kernel source took 6m4s with GNU tar vs 9.4 s with 64 workers (about 38.7x, derived from page data), and a 10 TB, 500K-file dataset took 10hr20m vs 44m39s with 32 workers (about 13.9x). No CPU, Go or GNU tar version, node count or scripts are given; the 1-worker run was slower than GNU tar.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-10-31 (15 stars, 0 open issues), MIT/Expat per the README; small enough (four packages) to vendor and modernize, but treat it as a sketch rather than a hardened archiver.
